description: This dataset is from a 1998 crossover study examining whether food presentation size influences meal intake and appetite in healthy adults. Men and women without overweight or obesity who were not dieting completed two counterbalanced visits and a follow-up session. At each visit, participants were served the same type of sandwich which was either presented as a full sandwich or cut up into 9 small rectangular pieces. Participants completed visual analog (VAS) scales to rate their hunger, thirst, fullness, desire to eat, and how much they thought they could eat (i.e., prospective consumption). They also rate the pleasantness of the taste and their desire to eat the sandwich before and after the meal. Intake was measured by weighing foods before and after the meal.

description: This dataset is from a 1990 crossover study examining how social context influences meal intake in healthy adults. Men and women without overweight or obesity completed two visits to the lab during which they either ate dinner alone or with three other individuals matched on gender and eating restraint. For the group condition, it was randomly assigned whether the other individuals were known friends or strangers. Participants were categorized as having heigh eating restraint or no using the Eating Inventory. Visual analog scales (VAS) were used to rate current mood, arousal state, hunger, thirst, fullness, and how much they thought they could eat (i.e., prospective consumption) before and after each meal. Participants were then presented with a spaghetti meal and water. Intake was measured by weighing foods before and after the meal.

description: This dataset is from a 1990 study investigating how age influences sensory-specific satiety (SSS), which is the decline in palatability of a food after consuming it. Individuals from four age groups (12-15 y; 22-35:45-60; 65-82) completed two counterbalanced lab visits, during which they consumed two different amounts (ad libitum or 300 g) of yogurt. Visual analog scales (VAS) were used to measure current state (e.g., hunger, thirst, nausea, fullness, and how much they thought they could eat (i.e., prospective consumption) before and after eating. SSS was measured using VAS ratings of pleasantness of foods before and after eating the yogurt. Intake was measured by weighing foods before and after the meal.

description: This dataset is from a 1992 study examining the effects of food deprivation on appetite, mood, and eating behavior in with inpatients from the Johns Hopkins Hospital Eating Disorder Unit and healthy community controls. Participants completed two counterbalanced dinner sessions in counterbalanced order, with at least one non-test day between sessions on alternating days during the first week of admission to the hospital. In the deprivation condition, inpatients started fasting after their 6pm dinner and healthy controls participants started fasting at 10 pm. The fast lasted until dinner the following day. In the non-deprivation condition, there was no fast. description: This dataset is from a 1991 study examining how the route of nutrient delivery — intravenous (IV) or intragastric (IG) infusion — affects appetite and food intake in men. Two separate samples of men received three infusion types on separate mornings: fat, carbohydrate, or isotonic saline in the morning. The IV group complete three sessions while the IG group completed six sessions to also test the rate of delivery (fast versus slow). Participants consumed lunch approximately 30 min after the infusion and dinner six hours post infusion. Visual analog scales (VAS) were used to assess hunger, thirst, fullness, prospective consumption, and nausea hourly. Blood collected from the IG group to assess physiological responses (note: only CCK data available). In addition to nutrient delivery, participants also completed a yogurt preload protocol over the course of three additional laboratory visits. In counterbalanced visits approximately 1 week apart, participants consumed a yogurt preload that was mostly carbohydrate, mostly fat, or no yogurt preload before eating lunch. Intake was measured by weighing foods before and after the consumption.

citation: Pearce, Alaina; Kral, Tanja V. E.; Roe, Liane S.; Rolls, Barbara (2026). Does nutrition information about the energy density of meals affect food intake in normal-weight women? A 2000 laboratory study [Data set]. Scholarsphere.
description: This dataset is from a 2000 crossover study investigating whether the energy density of foods affected energy intake when subjects were informed about the energy density of their meals. Forty normal-weight women ate breakfast, lunch, and dinner in the laboratory on three separate days. The entrée at each meal was varied in energy density to be either 1.25, 1.50, or 1.75 kcal/g (5.23, 6.28, or 7.32 kJ/g). Subjects were assigned to one of two groups. Subjects in the information group received a nutrition label with each meal, which showed the energy density of the entrée. Subjects in the no-information group did not receive any nutrition information. Before and after each meal, subjects completed visual analog scales (VAS) to rate their hunger, thirst, fullness, and how much they thought they could eat (i.e., prospective consumption). Also before and after each meal subjects rated that pleasantness of the taste and texture, perceived fat, saltiness, and sweetness, and estimated calories of the food. Intake was measured by weighing foods before and after the meal.

description: This dataset is from a 2000 crossover study investigating the influence of portion size on food and energy intake of a lunch meal. The study also examined whether the response to portion size depended on which person, the subject or the experimenter, determined the amount of food on the plate. Fifty-one men and women were served lunch 1 d/wk for 4 wk. Lunch included an entrée of macaroni and cheese consumed ad libitum. At each meal, subjects were presented with 1 of 4 portions of the entrée: 500, 625, 750, or 1000 g. One group of subjects received the portion on a plate, and a second group received it in a serving dish and took the amount they desired on their plates. Before and after lunch, participants rated their hunger, thirst, prospective consumption (how much food they thought they could eat), nausea, and fullness on visual analogue scales (VAS). Immediately before and after lunch, subjects were also presented with 10-g samples of macaroni and cheese, which were rated for palatability (pleasantness of appearance, odor, taste, and texture) with the use of VAS. Intake was measured by weighing foods before and after the meal.

description: This dataset is from three 2002 crossover experiments investigating the influence of plate size on intake of a lunch meal. On separate days, adults were served the same lunch menu but were given a different-sized plate. In the first study, 45 participants used each of three plate sizes (17, 22, or 26 cm) and served the main course from a large dish. In the second study, 30 participants received an equal amount of food presented on each of the two larger plates. In the third study, 44 participants used each of the three plates and selected from a buffet of five foods matched for energy density. Immediately before and after each experimental meal, participants rated their hunger, fullness, and prospective consumption (how much they thought they could eat) using visual analog scales (VAS).
